summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012; it allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in these sources.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people rose sharply in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, an average of one every 38 hours and a record, described as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. In April 2025 trans activists in Buenos Aires, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence, characterising the situation as chaotic and desperate.

Argentina's Supreme Court left standing in April 2025 the life sentence of Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that a cassation court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator is therefore currently not applied in this case.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws. Outright International's overview, updated 12 March 2026, nonetheless records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration in its current assessment.
tangentialFactors:
The narrowing of the Gender Identity Law as applied to minors is an executive measure, contested by legal experts as unconstitutional; its final judicial status is unresolved in these sources, and visitors should not assume either its validity or its repeal.

The travesticidio aggravating circumstance for gender-motivated homicide was removed by a cassation court in 2020 and the Supreme Court declined to restore it in 2025, so homicide of a trans person may be punished without that aggravator even as hate-crime monitoring records rising totals.

Recorded hate-crime totals derive from civil-society observation rather than a state count, so they likely understate incidence; the figure of 227 recorded offences in 2025 should be read as a floor.

Outright International's 2026 assessment marks deterioration across same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, a negative trend assessment set against the still-permissive text of Law 26.743.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change under Law 26.743 remains available to Argentine residents without surgery, hormone therapy or a court order, and the decree of February 2025 restricts gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors rather than for adults.

The February 2025 decree also governs where transgender people are held in prison; residents subject to that regime face the housing rules it sets, which legal experts have challenged as illegal and unconstitutional.

Argentina's 2010 marriage-equality law and national and provincial anti-discrimination statutes remain in force for residents, while the Outright International assessment of March 2026 records negative movement on organisation registration, affecting how LGBTIQ+ groups may register and operate.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio logged at least 227 sexual-orientation or gender-identity hate crimes in 2025, and trans advocacy organisations report that government policy has increased exposure to violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the courts have annulled, upheld or narrowed the February 2025 decree restricting gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in these sources; the inventory records only the legal experts' petition for judicial intervention.

The practical effect of the second February 2025 decree on where transgender detainees are housed is not specified in the inventory beyond its subject matter, and the conditions it produces are unsourced here.

No source in this inventory reports changes to passport or identity-document markers for adults, entry or visa screening that could expose a trans visitor's status, or facility and bathroom rules; those aspects of the record are not sourced in this pass.

The 227 hate-crime figure is a civil-society count and no official police or prosecutorial comparison for 2025 is provided, so the record-year claim rests on a single monitoring body.
